definition: a cleverly devised plan, scheme, or device, often artificial
memoryTip: Con-TRIVE-ance: a clever TRICK or device someone contrived.
correctPassage: The rescue hinged on a last-minute contrivance involving spare rope and a pulley.
wrongPassages: Her contrivance was so genuine that no one doubted a word she said.
After weeks of rest, the meadow returned to its natural contrivance.
The judge praised the witness for his honest contrivance under oath.

definition: to share a boundary with; touch along an edge
memoryTip: A-BUTT against: properties that butt up against each other.
correctPassage: Our backyard abuts a quiet creek that floods only in spring.
wrongPassages: Please abut the meeting until everyone has arrived.
His abut manners made the dinner conversation impossible.
Investors expected an abut forecast with exact quarterly numbers.

definition: persisting tirelessly; incapable of being worn out
memoryTip: In-de-FATIGUE-able: fatigue cannot stop you.
correctPassage: An indefatigable coach ran drills with the team until dusk every day.
wrongPassages: The indefatigable nap left her too groggy to finish the assignment.
After one easy practice, the squad declared itself fully indefatigable.
His indefatigable attitude meant he quit whenever the work got hard.

definition: written or published under a false name
memoryTip: PSEUDO + name: a fake name on the byline.
correctPassage: The columnist kept a pseudonymous blog to criticize her own industry.
wrongPassages: The choir sounded pseudonymous once the organ drowned every voice.
She filed a pseudonymous tax return listing her real legal name.
Ops hoped to make the outage pseudonymous by posting a public status update.

definition: to gently push; to lightly encourage toward an action
memoryTip: Elbow NUDGE: a light push that steers without force.
correctPassage: A reminder email can nudge students to finish the form before Friday.
wrongPassages: The wrecking ball gave the wall one final nudge and the building collapsed.
A single nudge of the throttle launched the rocket into orbit.
The shoreline looked nudge once weekend boats filled every slip.

definition: to voluntarily give up or stop claiming something
memoryTip: Re-LINQUISH: let go of a claim or hold (think relinquish the crown).
correctPassage: She refused to relinquish the keys until the lease was signed.
wrongPassages: He decided to relinquish the trophy by training harder than ever.
The brief was so relinquish that it ran thirty pages without a point.
Morning light looked relinquish through the narrow atrium skylight.

definition: to confirm or support as true; to give a personal guarantee
memoryTip: VOUCH for a friend: put your word behind their honesty.
correctPassage: Two former supervisors will vouch for his reliability on the job.
wrongPassages: Admin tried to vouch the complaint volume by hiding the contact form.
The icy trail felt vouch without a single handrail in sight.
She hoped to vouch the rumor by refusing to discuss it at all.

definition: providing additional help; serving as a secondary support
memoryTip: AUX jack: the extra, secondary connection that helps out.
correctPassage: Auxiliary nurses covered the night shift when the ward was short-staffed.
wrongPassages: The auxiliary conductor led the entire orchestra while the maestro sat silent.
They called the plan auxiliary because it replaced every other option.
Her auxiliary deposition was the only evidence the jury ever heard.

definition: to lead an attack, campaign, or major effort
memoryTip: Tip of the SPEAR: you go first and lead the charge.
correctPassage: A small committee will spearhead fundraising for the new library wing.
wrongPassages: He agreed to spearhead the project only by sitting silently in the back row.
The idle machine stayed spearhead through a surge that reset every device.
Fans called the ending spearhead for refusing to resolve any plotline.

definition: to draw out a response, fact, or reaction
memoryTip: E-LICIT draws it out—don't confuse with illicit (illegal).
correctPassage: The interviewer's silence helped elicit a more candid answer.
wrongPassages: Police seized the elicit shipment before it crossed the border.
Quants discarded the elicit factor that explained most of the variance.
The held fifth was elicit under a modulation that never returned.

definition: to assess the value, quality, or worth of something
memoryTip: APPRAise the price—assess value (not the same as praise).
correctPassage: A jeweler came to appraise the necklace before the insurance renewal.
wrongPassages: Fans rose to appraise the singer with a standing ovation.
The lab will appraise contamination by leaving samples unlabeled.
She hoped the coach would appraise her effort with a public speech.

definition: to perceive, detect, or recognize with care
memoryTip: DIS-cern: sift carefully until you can tell things apart.
correctPassage: Only a trained ear can discern the slight change in pitch.
wrongPassages: The firm tried to discern open tickets by auto-closing anything over thirty days old.
They billed discern time by rounding every six-minute block upward.
The tide gauge's discern needle had been frozen mid-scale for months.

definition: clearly visible; attracting notice
memoryTip: Con-SPIC-uous: easy to SEE (Latin spicere) because it stands out.
correctPassage: His bright red jacket made him conspicuous in the gray crowd.
wrongPassages: She kept the papers conspicuous in a locked drawer no one ever opened.
The motif sounded conspicuous after brass buried it completely.
His quiet, camouflaged outfit was designed to be as conspicuous as possible.

definition: to formally declare that one is giving something up
memoryTip: Re-NOUNCE: publicly announce you are giving it up.
correctPassage: She chose to renounce the inheritance and donate it instead.
wrongPassages: Reviewers called the stats renounce after the reanalysis matched the paper.
The empty dock looked renounce with loaders parked for a decade.
He hoped to renounce the award by accepting it on live television.

definition: a minor weakness or harmless eccentricity
memoryTip: A little FOIBLE is a foil-able flaw—minor, not fatal.
correctPassage: His only foible was humming while he graded late at night.
wrongPassages: The structural foible cracked the foundation from corner to corner.
Critics praised her foible leadership for saving the company in a crisis.
The only foible in the bridge design was a missing support beam.

definition: to express disapproval or disappointment; blame
memoryTip: Re-PROACH: approach someone again—with blame, not praise.
correctPassage: There was quiet reproach in the way she asked why he was late.
wrongPassages: Fans offered loud reproach that sounded exactly like a standing ovation.
The empty dock looked reproach with ramps chained up for years.
Her letter of reproach thanked him warmly for every favor he had done.

definition: showing scorn or deep disrespect
memoryTip: Full of CONTEMPT—scornful, looking down on someone.
correctPassage: His contemptuous shrug made it clear he thought the plan was foolish.
wrongPassages: The orchard looked contemptuous after hail stripped every tree.
She gave a contemptuous smile that radiated pure admiration.
He called the puzzle contemptuous after solving it in under a minute.

definition: very surprising or astonishing
memoryTip: Makes you START (jump)—so surprising you flinch.
correctPassage: The most startling finding was that sleep alone cut errors in half.
wrongPassages: Nothing about the predictable ending felt startling to anyone in the room.
The empty stand looked startling after packing, with only chalk marks left.
Voters tabled the startling tax that every rider had already calmly expected.

definition: to fail to give a true impression of; to contradict
memoryTip: Be-LIE: the surface lies about what is really underneath.
correctPassage: His calm tone belied how nervous he felt before the exam.
wrongPassages: I fully belie the witness after checking every date in her story.
She closed the ticket as belie while action items still had no owners.
Fans found the remaster belie for files identical to the old CD.

definition: peculiar to an individual; highly distinctive
memoryTip: IDIO + quirks: your personal odd habits and style.
correctPassage: Her idiosyncratic color code made the spreadsheet unreadable to others.
wrongPassages: Everyone followed the same idiosyncratic checklist issued by headquarters.
The salt flat stayed idiosyncratic under a model with permanent drought.
The tripwire was idiosyncratic: set past any value the logs could store.
